newsitem.title: CROATIA: FEATURE - Croatia holds exhibition of antique stuffed frogs.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Croatia holds exhibition of antique stuffed frogs.

text.p: ZAGREB, March 23 (Zagreb) - The sound of croaking fills the air as the visitor approaches.

The "Enchanted Swamp", an exhibition currently on show in a tent in central Zagreb, features more than 500 frogs stuffed almost a century ago by taxidermist Ferenz Mere, who displayed them as humans at work and play.

Scenes in 21 lighted glass cabinets depict frogs playing cards, rowing boats, swaying to the beat of a barn dance, misbehaving in a school classroom and pulling teeth from a dental patient with giant pliers.
Who Mere was and what inspired him is still much of a mystery.
What is known is confined to two articles published in a Croatian newspaper in 1964.
The Arena weekly said Mere was born to a well-to-do family in 1878 in Sombor, Serbia where he finished his education and later ran a brick factory.
After World War One he sold the plant and took to farming. Apparently this is when he became interested in frogs living in numerous nearby swamps.
"He wondered how to preserve the frogs whom he thought were very similar to humans and arrived at this original idea," the paper quoted his friend Rudolf Cirkli as saying.
Cirkli said Mere began his work in 1910 and it took him a decade to complete 40 "grotesque" scenes containing 1,000 frogs, half of which have decayed beyond repair.
By World War Two the collection had been shown in 46 European cities from Sweden to Italy.
The current owner, Ivan Medvesek, said his parents bought the collection in 1964 after reading that someone had stored it in a basement.
"They thought it was a unique thing that could be shown around the world," he said.
His family built a travelling show called "Fantasy in Froggyland" but business faded and the show was closed, only to be revived three decades later in Croatia.
"Many have wondered about the special technique Mere used to stuff the frogs," Medvesek said, explaining it was done with wire put through the mouth which left the skin intact.
Mere had a talent for detail, including in his displays tiny tools, furniture and accessories.
"I was amazed to see how much a frog can look like a human," wrote one woman in the exhibition's visitors' book.

Medvesek admits that there haven't been too many visitors to his exhibition, something he attributes to a lack of advertising and Croatia's relatively modest standard of living -- admission is $4 for adults and $1.90 for children.
"I have become a media personality thanks to the frogs," he said, mentioning plans to take the exhibit to Germany, Italy and the United States.
